result:
None of the three solutions gives the correct value, as far as I can tell. I derived the maximum as 2^999 − 2^499, and Solution 3 is the closest of the three.

**Upper bound.** An intersecting family contains at most one set from each complementary pair {A, Aᶜ}, so |P| ≤ 2^999.

Condition 3 combined with condition 2 forces A ∩ A′ ≠ ∅ for every A in P. That means A contains some full pair {t, 1001−t}.

Call a set a transversal if it takes exactly one element from each of the 500 pairs. There are 2^500 transversals. None of them can be in P, since a transversal has no full pair. The complement of a transversal is its reflection, so the transversals fall into 2^499 complementary pairs {A, Aᶜ}. P can contain neither set of any such pair. Hence |P| ≤ 2^999 − 2^499.

**Construction.**
- Take every set with more than 500 elements. Any two of these intersect, and the family is closed under reflection.
- Among the 500-element sets, the only disjoint pairs are complementary pairs. From each complementary pair that is not a transversal pair, choose one set, and choose reflection-compatibly. If A′ = A, either A or Aᶜ works. Otherwise take the orbit {A, A′} together. A and A′ intersect because A contains a full pair.
- The count is (2^1000 − C(1000,500))/2 + (C(1000,500) − 2^500)/2 = 2^999 − 2^499.

**Checking the solutions.**
- Solution 1 gives 2^999. This is impossible, because the transversal pairs cannot be included.
- Solution 2 gives 3·2^997. This is far too small. Its "maximality" argument is not actually proved.
- Solution 3 gives (2^1000 − C(1000,500))/2 + C(998,498). This is valid but not maximal. It adds only the 500-element sets containing one fixed pair, whereas far more can be added.

CHOICE: 3
